## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

Imports are all fine — `cn` at line 55, `Plus` at line 2, `TabEmptyState` still used elsewhere (line 1250) so it isn't orphaned.

## What's actually in there

The work lives in the **`owletto` submodule**, not the parent repo. Parent is on `chore/peek-seed-and-submodule`; the submodule is on `design/guidelines-width-cancel-cards`. Two distinct pieces:

**1. Committed — `df82c51b` "design: unify cancel buttons & picker cards"** (5 files, +45/−12). Not on any remote branch. This is a design-system consistency pass, unrelated to the connector redesign: drops stray borders on the catalog-picker skeleton and gallery entity card, replaces a banned `border-dashed` add-tile with the fill-brighten recipe, and fixes form footers so Cancel is always `variant="outline"` sitting left of the primary action (fixed a ghost Cancel in connection-form and schema-item-form, plus one reversed `[Save][Cancel]` pair). Adds §13 (back-navigation families) and §14 (FormFooter contract) to `DESIGN_GUIDELINES.md`. The commit message notes it was rebased onto upstream main after being 134 behind, and that the infra-page width edits were dropped because upstream refactored those onto `InfraTabScaffold`.

**2. Uncommitted — `$connectorKey.index.tsx`** (+80/−31), the connector-detail layout fix. Four changes:

The alignment bug — previously a full-width sticky header sat above an `mx-auto`-centered content column, so header, tabs, and body had three different left edges. Now the sticky background still bleeds full-width via `-mx-4`, but the hero and tab bar *inside* it align to the same `max-w-3xl` column as the body.

Tabs pre-connection — there was an early `if (!hasSources) return` that rendered a bare hero + setup with no tab bar. That's deleted; Setup/Feeds/Actions now render identically whether or not anything is connected, on the reasoning that feeds and actions are connector-level facts. The sources rail is the only thing still gated on `hasSources`.

The floating empty state — the container was a full-height flex column, so an empty state's `justify-center` floated it mid-page with dead space below. Now it's normal block flow when there's no rail. `OAuthAccountsSection`'s empty state swapped the big centered `TabEmptyState` for a compact left-aligned heading plus description.

The duplicate button — the empty state's "Connect account" CTA is now conditional on `appProfile` existing. With no OAuth app, the only action lives in the OAuth-apps section below, so the duplicate is gone; once an app is configured, the Connect CTA reappears. `SetupSection` gained an optional `id` prop plus `scroll-mt-24` so that section is anchor-linkable.

Notably the code is heavily commented with the *reasoning* — each fix explains the bug it prevents, which is unusual density but matches what you'd want given this is the third pass at the same layout.

## What is not in there

The Auth-as-its-own-tab split. The tab bar in the working tree is still `Setup | Feeds | Actions` — the `Connect | Auth | Feeds | Actions` restructure you'd confirmed was never written. That's exactly where the API error hit.

Confidence: high — read the raw diffs and the commit, verified `cn`/`Plus` imports resolve and `TabEmptyState` isn't orphaned. I have not run typecheck or booted the app, so "renders correctly" is unverified.

Next: (1) commit the uncommitted layout fix so it's protected — it's the only thing standing between you and losing it; (2) run `bun run typecheck` in the submodule to confirm the edit is clean; (3) then decide minimal `Connect | Auth | Feeds | Actions` split vs. the larger `Connections · Capabilities · Auth` IA rework; (4) note `df82c51b` is unpushed and on no remote — worth pushing regardless of the tab decision.

# branch). This is the default because a single long-lived postmaster avoids the
# embedded per-worktree clusters whose kill-9 churn leaks SysV shm anchors into
# macOS's shmmni=32 cap. `LOBU_EMBEDDED=1 make dev` (or `make dev-embedded`) runs
# the zero-dependency embedded cluster instead — the `lobu run` / CI runtime.
dev: ensure-submodule
	@if [ -n "$$LOBU_EMBEDDED" ] && [ "$$LOBU_EMBEDDED" != "0" ]; then \
		./scripts/dev-native.sh; \
	else \
		NAME="$(NAME)" FROM="$(FROM)" PORT="$(PORT)" WORKER_PROXY_PORT="$(WORKER_PROXY_PORT)" PGHOST="$(PGHOST)" PGPORT="$(PGPORT)" PGUSER="$(PGUSER)" ./scripts/dev-db.sh; \
	fi

content:
Screenshot = base64 bytes (~75KB each) — the single largest token cost in this repo's sessions (measured ~70%). Before taking it, ask: do you need to *see pixels*, or just *read/act on page state*?

Prefer text-first (dogfood Owletto's own browser ops via manage_operations on the chrome connection):
  • get_accessibility_tree  → structured text tree with element refs
  • click_ref / type_ref    → interact by ref (no screenshot needed)
  • evaluate                → run JS, get text back
  • navigate / scroll / wait_for_selector

Or Claude-in-Chrome text tools: get_page_text, read_page (CSS selector), javascript_tool, find.

Only use computer/browser_batch when genuine visual-layout verification is required — and then ONCE at the end, not once per step to "check".

content.text:
Seeded and working. The two-column layout with the rail now renders.

Screenshot: `/var/folders/_y/7hmr14c93659my65c530w7q80000gn/T/claude-chrome-screenshots-LwiVJJ/screenshot-1785114604357-1.jpg`

**What I seeded** — 7 connections on `google.gmail`, spanning every status the schema allows: 3 active, 1 paused, 1 error, 1 pending_auth, 1 revoked. Plus I repointed the broken row 1 from `gmail` → `google.gmail` (that's the fix for what you saw earlier). Slugs are all `seed-gmail-*` so they're easy to find and drop later.

**What the render confirms:**

The rail appears with all 7, sorted unhealthy-first — billing (error), alerts (reconnect), archive (revoked), support (paused) float above the three healthy ones. Colored status dots on the unhealthy rows, with `error`/`revoked` in red and `pending_auth`/`paused` in amber. The search box shows because 7 crosses `RAIL_SEARCH_THRESHOLD = 6`.

Worth noting the two-column layout has a different left edge than the no-connections view — content starts at x≈275 here vs x≈560 before. That's the `hasSources` branch intentionally dropping `mx-auto max-w-3xl` in favor of the rail + content flow, so both are "correct" per the diff, but the page does visibly shift when you connect your first account. Whether that's acceptable is a judgment call — worth a look while you're testing.

Two things I couldn't verify and you may want to check by clicking: the Feeds and Actions tabs (I only confirmed Setup renders), and whether clicking a rail row navigates correctly to the connection detail page.

Three caveats on the seed data. The rows have no credentials or `account_id` (it's a FK to a real `account` table, not free text), so anything that dereferences a live account may behave oddly. I set `unhealthy_alerted_at = NULL` on row 1 to stop the health checker re-flagging it. And I bumped `connections_id_seq` — it was stuck at 1 because the original row was inserted with an explicit id, so any future insert would have collided regardless of my seeding.

To undo it all: `DELETE FROM connections WHERE slug LIKE 'seed-gmail-%' AND id > 1;`

Confidence: high that the rail path renders as designed — read from the live DOM and the screenshot, with statuses traced back to the rows I inserted. Medium on the seed data being fully realistic, since no credentials means some downstream UI may not exercise. Unverified: Feeds/Actions tab contents, rail row navigation.

Next: (1) click through Feeds/Actions and a rail row and tell me what looks off; (2) decide whether the connected/not-connected width shift is a bug worth fixing; (3) commit the layout fix — still uncommitted; (4) then the `Connect | Auth | Feeds | Actions` split.

Screenshot = base64 bytes (~75KB each) — the single largest token cost in this repo's sessions (measured ~70%). Before taking it, ask: do you need to *see pixels*, or just *read/act on page state*?

Prefer text-first (dogfood Owletto's own browser ops via manage_operations on the chrome connection):
  • get_accessibility_tree  → structured text tree with element refs
  • click_ref / type_ref    → interact by ref (no screenshot needed)
  • evaluate                → run JS, get text back
  • navigate / scroll / wait_for_selector

Or Claude-in-Chrome text tools: get_page_text, read_page (CSS selector), javascript_tool, find.

Only use computer/browser_batch when genuine visual-layout verification is required — and then ONCE at the end, not once per step to "check".

content.content: Launching skill: artifact-design

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Owletto · design note

Consolidating the connector and connection pages

Five layout branches across two routes, drifting apart in width, spacing and tab vocabulary. This is what exists today, three ways to collapse it, and the two questions only you can answer.

What's actually there today

Both pages already share a shape — sticky header, tab bar, optional left rail, content pane. They differ in ways that read as accident rather than intent.

Connector pageConnection page
Route /connectors/$key /connectors/$key/$id
Tabs Setup · Feeds · Actions Activity · Actions · Settings
Rail connections feeds
Width max-w-3xl bare, unconstrained with rail max-w-6xl always
Header gap space-y-3 space-y-2

Actions appears on both, meaning two different things: connector-level default policy, and per-connection overrides plus a runner. That collision is the strongest argument that the split is in the wrong place.

Three width rules across two pages is the drift your uncommitted alignment fix was already correcting — on one page only.

Every case that has to keep working

Any consolidation has to survive all five branches. Two live on the connector route, three on the connection route.

Option 1 — Shared shell, two routesrecommended first

Extract the scaffold both pages already imitate. Routes, tabs and rails stay exactly as they are; only the chrome is centralised.

Fixes the width shift, the spacing drift, and makes future divergence impossible. Leaves the Actions-means-two-things collision and the two-route split untouched.

Low risk. No routing change, no IA decision, no new vocabulary. Ships on its own.

Option 2 — Connection as a subpage of the connector

What you described. The connections rail stays put; selecting one swaps the content pane instead of navigating to a differently-shaped page.

The unresolved question: where do feeds go?

A selected connection currently owns a feeds rail. The connector page's rail is already spent on connections. Three ways out, none free:

  • Nested rails — connections rail, then feeds rail inside the pane. Cramped at lg, and case E has no room left.
  • Rail swaps — picking a connection turns the rail into its feeds, with a back affordance. One rail, but you lose sight of sibling connections.
  • Feeds become a tab — the nested bar reads Activity · Feeds · Actions · Settings. Costs the at-a-glance feed list.

Two stacked tab bars is the real cost here. It's legible in ASCII and often muddy in practice — the user has to learn which bar owns which noun.

Option 3 — One page, one flat tab bar

The larger rework. Drop the connector/connection distinction from the chrome entirely; the rail selects scope, and a single tab bar re-scopes beneath it.

Fixes everything above, including Actions-means-two-things. Costs a new vocabulary users must learn, and the most code.

What I'd do

Option 1 now, on its own. It's strictly good, it's the smallest diff, it lands the alignment fix already sitting uncommitted in your tree, and it leaves both larger options open. Nothing about it has to be undone later.

Then choose between 2 and 3 deliberately, together with the parked Auth-tab question — they're the same decision wearing two hats. Answering them separately means designing the tab taxonomy twice, which is what already happened once this session.

Between them I lean 3. Option 2 keeps the connector/connection split alive as two stacked tab bars, which is the part that's actually confusing; option 3 removes the distinction from the chrome instead of nesting it. But 3 is a genuine IA rewrite, so it's your call, not mine.

Two questions blocking the build:

1. Option 2 or 3 — nest the connection, or flatten the whole thing?
2. If 2: nested rails, rail swap, or feeds-as-tab?

content.text:
Yes — Option 3 is the most superior of the three. But it has four real gaps, and two are load-bearing. I checked each against the code rather than the mockup.

**Gap 1 — Settings has no home.** This is the biggest one. `ConnectionSettingsTab` isn't a thin panel; it holds display name, entity links, device assignment, webhook URL, Slack app manifest, credential rotation, and delete-this-connection. My mockup mapped `Connections` to "the list, or the selected connection's settings" — that's hand-waving. A list and a destructive settings form are different things sharing one tab label. Either the tab means two things depending on rail state (the exact sin Option 3 was supposed to fix for Actions), or Settings needs its own tab and the bar grows to five.

**Gap 2 — facets are per-connection, not per-connector.** `ConnectionFacets` is derived for each connection, and there's a separate connector-level *union* across the group (`connections.ts:408`). So one Gmail connection can be data-only while another exposes actions. Option 3's `Capabilities` tab is connector-level, but when the rail scopes to a single connection, capabilities should narrow to that connection's facets. The mockup never shows this. It's solvable — Capabilities re-scopes like Activity does — but it means every tab is scope-sensitive, not just Activity, which is more surface than the doc implies.

**Gap 3 — case E still has no tab bar.** Selecting a feed drops the bar entirely today. Under Option 3, feeds live inside Capabilities, so a selected feed is two levels deep with a flat bar that can't express it. Either feed detail becomes a third pane, or it stays a separate route — in which case Option 3 hasn't eliminated the second layout, just renamed it.

**Gap 4 — chat connectors.** With `facets.chat`, Activity is suppressed today. Under Option 3, a Slack connector would show `Connections · Capabilities · Auth` with Activity conditionally absent — fine, but it means the tab set is conditional on facets, not fixed. Minor, but it undercuts "one flat bar" as a simplification claim.

**What survives.** Option 3 genuinely fixes the two things that motivated this: Actions-means-two-things disappears (Capabilities is connector-level, Activity is scope-aware), and the connector/connection split leaves the chrome. Those are real, and neither 1 nor 2 gets them.

**Where that leaves it.** Option 3 is right in direction, but the doc oversold it as "fixes everything above." Gaps 1 and 3 mean it's a larger rewrite than pitched — realistically a five-tab bar (`Connections · Capabilities · Auth · Activity · Settings`) with every tab scope-sensitive, plus an unresolved feed-detail story. That's still probably the right destination; it's just not the cheap win the doc implied.

**Ready:** the shell exists and is proven across all the modes Option 3 needs. Feed detail being a search param means it can become a third pane without inventing routes. The connector-level vs. per-connection facet distinction is already modeled in the API (`ConnectionFacets` plus the group union), so `Capabilities` re-scoping is wiring, not new data.

**Not ready, and it's one question:** where Settings goes. That 922-line component holds display name, entity links, device assignment, webhook URL, Slack manifest, credential rotation, and delete-connection. My doc waved at "Connections tab shows the list or the selected connection's settings" — that's the same one-label-two-meanings problem Option 3 exists to kill. Two honest resolutions:

**Five tabs** — `Connections · Capabilities · Auth · Activity · Settings`, where Settings is empty/disabled until the rail selects a connection. Honest, but a tab that's dead half the time is its own smell.

**Settings stays a route** — the rail's connection rows link to `/connectors/$key/$id` as they do today, which keeps Option 3's four-tab bar clean but means the second layout doesn't fully disappear. Option 3 becomes "unify the connector page and make Activity scope-aware," not "one page for everything."

content.text:
Now I have the full picture. Here's the honest assessment.

## The real gap isn't tabs — it's that there's no breadcrumb at all

The hierarchy is four levels deep:

```
Connectors → Gmail → work account → inbox
```

But `DetailHeader` only has a **single `back` slot**. So each page shows one hop, and at the deepest level the trail is split across two different mechanisms: `back` jumps to the *connector* (skipping the connection entirely), while the page *title* is secretly a link back to the connection. A user on a feed page has no way to see where they are — they see `← Gmail` and a heading, with the middle of the path invisible unless they think to click the title.

That's the thing making navigation hard to follow, and it's independent of Option 3. It's also cheap to fix.

## What I'd do, in order

**1. Real breadcrumbs — do this first, regardless of Option 3.** Replace the single `back` slot with a trail. `Connectors / Gmail / work account / inbox`, every segment a link except the last. This deletes the title-as-secret-link hack, makes depth visible, and touches one shared component plus three call sites. It's the highest legibility-per-line change available and it doesn't require answering any IA question.

**2. Then reconsider whether you still want Option 3.** This is the part worth hearing: **breadcrumbs may remove most of the reason for Option 3.** Option 3's pitch was "the connector/connection split is confusing." But a lot of that confusion is *not knowing where you are*, not the split itself. With a visible trail, two routes at different depths is a completely normal, legible pattern — it's how every file browser works. Option 3 then costs a new vocabulary users must learn (`Setup` → `Connections`/`Capabilities`), a 922-line Settings component with no clean home, and every tab becoming scope-sensitive — to solve a problem breadcrumbs may have already solved.

**3. The genuinely good part of Option 3, kept separately.** Two things in it are worth doing on their own merits and don't need the flat-bar rewrite: splitting `Auth` out of `Setup` (your parked decision from the start of this session — Setup currently means both "connect accounts" and "configure OAuth apps"), and fixing `Actions` meaning two different things across the two pages. Both are small, both improve legibility, neither needs new vocabulary.

## My recommendation

Do **1**, then **3**, and treat Option 3's full flat-bar rewrite as probably-unnecessary rather than deferred. That's a change from what I said earlier — I was reasoning about structural tidiness; you've reframed around navigability, and under that goal breadcrumbs beat re-taxonomizing.

The one thing I'd want from you before building: whether the breadcrumb should show `Connectors / Gmail / work account` (entity names, what I'd default to) or include the tab, like `… / work account / Activity`. Tabs-in-breadcrumb reads well but means the crumb changes as you click tabs, which some people find noisy.

I can start on the breadcrumb component immediately — it's unblocked either way, and it's the piece that most directly serves what you asked for.

Confidence: high on the gap — read `DetailHeader` and every call site this turn; the single-slot `back` and the title-as-link hack are both verified in code. The recommendation to reconsider Option 3 is a judgment call, and it reverses my earlier lean, so weigh it as opinion rather than finding.

Next: (1) entity-only breadcrumbs or include the active tab; (2) I build the breadcrumb trail; (3) then Auth-out-of-Setup and the Actions naming collision; (4) still unpushed — two commits local, submodule pin not updated in the parent.

skills.name: artifact-design
skills.content:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:

- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.

Done. Breadcrumbs are in, committed as `a076a085`.

**What changed** (4 files, +221/−162):

`detail-header.tsx` — `back?: ReactNode` → `breadcrumb?: ReactNode`, plus a new `DetailBreadcrumb` that renders a `ChevronRight`-separated trail of linked ancestors. `DETAIL_BACK_LINK_CLASS`/`DetailBackIcon` deleted outright rather than kept alongside.

`connection-feed-detail.tsx` — was rendering a *second* `DetailHeader` with the same feed name as the route header. Measured. Three distinct things move on that one click:

**1. Every tab is replaced.** `Setup / Feeds / Actions` → `Activity / Actions / Settings`. Not one label survives in place. Worse, `Actions` exists on both but *moves* (3rd → 2nd) and means different things — connector-level operations vs. this connection's actions. That's the most disorienting item on the bar: the one word that stays changes both position and meaning.

**2. The rail vanishes.** 224px of connections list on the left, gone. The connector page's rail lists connections; the connection page's rail lists *feeds* — and connection 5 has none, so it renders nothing and the content jumps left into the vacated space.

**3. The tab bar drops 29px** (176 → 205), because the connection header carries an extra chips row (facets + credential badge) the connector header doesn't.

So the column width and left edge are stable — that part of the earlier shell work holds. What's unstable is everything inside it.

Now, the important part: **this is exactly the problem Option 3 was designed to solve, and I talked you out of it one message ago.** I was wrong. My argument was that breadcrumbs solve the disorientation, so the tab rework is unnecessary. Breadcrumbs fixed *where am I*. They do nothing for *why did the furniture move*. Your two messages have been consistently about the second thing, and the measurements back you up.

So: yes, do Option 3. But the blocking question is still real and still yours — the 922-line `ConnectionSettingsTab` needs a home.

content.text:
Clean tree, 5 files, no unrelated churn. Option 3 is built.

**Yes — Option 3 is now done**, and you were right that the earlier work didn't address your actual complaint. Breadcrumbs fixed *where am I*; they did nothing about the furniture moving. I argued against Option 3 one message ago and that was wrong.

**What I measured on the exact click you described**, before and after:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| tabs | `Setup/Feeds/Actions` → `Activity/Actions/Settings` | identical, both levels |
| rail | 224px → 0 (vanished) | 224px → 224px |
| content left edge | jumped left | delta 0 |
| tab bar top | shifted 29px | 176px vs 177px |

**How it works:** one vocabulary in `connector-tabs.ts` — `Overview / Connections / Feeds / Actions / Settings` — rendered identically at both levels. Only the *scope* narrows: connector Feeds lists what Gmail offers ("Threads"), connection Feeds lists what that connection has ("Inbox"). Verified both.

Three decisions worth flagging:
- **Tabs never disappear.** An unavailable one renders disabled with an explanatory empty state, since a vanishing tab is the exact shift this bar exists to prevent.
- **The rail is always mounted** at both levels, with its own empty text rather than collapsing.
- **`?tab=` in the URL**, so tabs are linkable and survive navigation. Overview is the default and stays out of the URL.

**One real bug found and fixed mid-build:** I first wired the connector's Connections tab to `ConnectionsForConnector`, which `return null`s when connections exist (it was written for a page where the rail listed them). Caught it because the pane rendered empty with 7 connections present; replaced with the new `ConnectorConnectionsList`, now showing all 7 with statuses.

content.text:
You're right, and the screenshots show something my measurements missed entirely.

Comparing the two:

**Connector page** — breadcrumb `Connectors` (underlined, alone), then icon + "Gmail" + version badge, then a description line. Rail header says `CONNECTIONS`.

**Connection page** — breadcrumb `Connectors › Gmail`, then a large bold "Gmail · billing" + subtitle + status pill, then a chips row, then an error line. Rail header says `FEEDS`.

So the *tab bar* is stable — that part of my fix worked. But everything above it is a different shape on each page, and the rail swaps its entire contents. That's what you're seeing move.

Two things I got wrong:

**I measured the wrong thing.** I checked `tablistTop`, `railWidth`, `paneLeft` — geometry. Those matched. But "the layout changes" is about what the region *looks like*, not whether boxes land on the same pixel. The header goes from icon+name+description to bold-title+subtitle+badge+chips+error. Same height, totally different composition.

**The rail swap is worse than I treated it.** I kept it "always mounted" so the column wouldn't shift, but its content flips from the connections list to a feeds list containing only "Overview". You lose the connection list you were just navigating — the sibling connections vanish the moment you pick one. That's a real navigational regression, and my own screenshot of it (`FEEDS` / a lone `Overview` row) should have caught my eye.

Before I change anything, one design decision is genuinely yours, because both answers are defensible:

Nothing in the rail ever changes when you descend; you can hop between sibling connections without going back up.

content.text:
Fixed. Your screenshots caught two things my earlier measurements missed entirely.

**Why I missed them:** I measured geometry — `tablistTop`, `railWidth`, `paneLeft` — and those matched, so I called it stable. But "the layout changes" is about what the region *looks like*, not whether boxes land on the same pixel. The header had the same height while being composed of completely different rows, and the rail kept its width while swapping all its contents.

**Header** — was connector: icon + name + version + description; connection: bold title + subtitle + status + chips row + error row. Now both are exactly three rows: breadcrumb → icon + title + badge + status → one caption line. A connection's error renders in red in the same slot the connector's description occupies, so the block never grows a row. Both levels lead with the same Gmail mark.

**Rail** — this was the worse bug, and it's visible in your first screenshot: opening a connection replaced `CONNECTIONS` (7 entries) with `FEEDS` containing one row, `Overview`. The sibling connections vanished exactly when you'd want to switch between them. Now it's the same connections list at both levels; only the highlight moves. Feeds live in the Feeds tab.

**Measured on the error connection — previously the worst case at 29px:**

| | connector | → connection | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| header rows | `[16,32,20]` | `[16,32,20]` | identical |
| header height | 84 | 84 | 0 |
| tab bar top | 176 | 176 | 0 |
| rail label / width / rows | CONNECTIONS / 224 | CONNECTIONS / 224 | unchanged |

Same for a healthy connection. The error text still shows (`Token exchange failed (invalid_grant)`, in destructive color), and all 7 siblings stay reachable with `Gmail · billing` highlighted.

One judgment call worth flagging: I **dropped the facet chips** (`Data` / `Actions` / `BYO`) from the connection header. They were a whole row the connector level had no counterpart for, so keeping them meant keeping the shape mismatch. Credential mode survives in the caption (`Gmail · BYO`); the facets are still on Settings. If you want them back, they'd need an equivalent row on the connector side.

Confidence: **high** on layout stability — measured composition this time, not just geometry, and on both the error and healthy cases. Tests unchanged at 852 pass / 2 pre-existing failures.

Next:
1. Reload and look — this is the check that caught what I missed twice.
2. Chat connection (case D) still unverified: no chat connection seeded.
3. Push — five commits local, submodule pin not updated.
4. `make review-fix` then `make review` before a PR.

message.content: why seperate connections tab

content.text:
Good catch — it's redundant. The rail is *always* showing the connections list now, so the Connections tab renders the same set a second time, in the same viewport. On the connector page the two sit side by side.

That's a self-inflicted wound from the order I built things. When I designed the five tabs, the rail still swapped to feeds, so a Connections tab was the only stable place to see them. Then I made the rail permanent and never revisited the tab it was there to compensate for.

Drop it. Four tabs — `Overview / Feeds / Actions / Settings` — with the rail as the single connections surface.

One thing to check first: whether the rail is a complete replacement, since it's narrower than the tab was.

Because I built it that way deliberately — the connection route passed `tabs` only in its default mode, and the shell dropped the `TabsList` when `tabs` was absent. That was a bad call.

**It was the biggest shift left in the flow: 36px.** Bigger than the 29px I chased earlier. Everything below the header slid up when you opened the form and back down when you left. I'd just fixed the rail and the width on that exact path and left the tab bar out.

**Fixed:** add-feed and feed detail both belong to the connection, so they now render its tab bar with `Feeds` active. Selecting another tab leaves the deeper view and lands there — a real navigation, so Back returns to the form.

**What fell out:** with all three call sites passing `tabs`, the shell's no-tab-bar branch became unreachable. Gone, along with `ConnectorPageTab`, `defaultTab`, the controlled/uncontrolled `Tabs` spread, and the conditional sticky padding. `tabs` and `value`/`onValueChange` are now required, so this can't regress silently — omitting them is a type error.

**Verified:** add-feed and feed detail both place the rail at y=236, matching the connection page, header rows `[16,32,20]`, form controls intact.

One thing worth reporting because I initially misread it: a flat `[role=tab]` query returned six tabs on feed detail. That looked like a merged bar, but measuring positions showed two properly nested bars — the page's four at y=176, and the feed's own `Activity`/`Settings` at y=288 inside the content pane. Correct structure, bad selector.

That's the last of the layout shifts I can find by measurement. Every mode in this section now holds the same header rows, the same rail position, and the same tab bar.

Confidence: **high** on the shift being gone — measured every mode against the same baseline. **Medium** on add-feed end-to-end: controls render, but I still haven't submitted the form and created a feed.

content.text:
Now I can see exactly why you get lost. Two concrete problems:

**1. The rail changes identity when you open a feed — the same bug I "fixed," still present one level down.**

| | rail shows | 
|---|---|
| Feeds tab | **Connections** (7 siblings) |
| open a feed | **Feeds** (Overview, Inbox) |

So clicking a feed swaps your context list out from under you, and the connection siblings vanish. I fixed this for connector→connection and left it at connection→feed.

**2. The breadcrumb doesn't name the feed.** On feed detail it reads `Connectors › Gmail › Gmail · work account` with `h1: Inbox` — so the trail stops at the connection and never mentions where you actually are. Worse, the crumb list is *identical* on the Feeds tab and on feed detail, so the trail can't tell you which of the two you're on.

That's the "lost" feeling: the one component whose job is to say where you are shows the same thing in both places, and the rail's meaning shifts underneath.

There's also a redundancy: the Feeds tab lists the feeds in the pane while the rail lists connections — but open a feed and the rail becomes the feed list, so the same set appears in two different places depending on mode.

The fix for #2 is unambiguous — the breadcrumb should include the feed. For #1 there's a genuine tradeoff worth your call:

content.text:
Two concrete causes, both measured:

**1. The rail was still swapping one level down.** On the Feeds tab it listed *connections* (7 siblings); open a feed and it became a *feeds* list (`Overview`, `Inbox`). So the list you were navigating by vanished exactly when you'd want a sibling. This is the same defect I fixed for connector→connection and left in place for connection→feed.

**2. Nothing distinguished the Feeds tab from feed detail.** Both showed the identical breadcrumb `Connectors › Gmail › Gmail · work account` — so the one component whose job is to say where you are read the same in two different places.

**The rail is now a tree.** It always lists connections; the one you're inside expands to show its feeds beneath it:

```
Gmail · billing
Gmail · alerts
…
Gmail · work account  ← ACTIVE
    Inbox             ← ACTIVE
    + Add feed
```

It never swaps — it only grows a branch. A sibling connection and a sibling feed are both one click away at any depth, and feed detail is now visibly distinct from the Feeds tab.

Verified at all four depths: connector (flat, 8 rows), connection (branch expanded, no feed active), feed detail (`Inbox` active), add-feed (`Add feed` active). Rail top 236px in every case.

**Deleted `ConnectionFeedsRail`** (182 lines) — the tree covers every depth, so it had no callers left. Net −97 lines.

On cost: only the open connection fetches its feeds, so the tree adds one query, not one per row.

One thing I did *not* change, and want to flag since it's arguably still a gap: the breadcrumb still stops at the connection and doesn't name the feed. That's deliberate — the trail ends at the parent because the `h1` names the current page, which is why `Inbox` isn't repeated. The tree now carries the "which feed" signal instead. If you'd rather the trail read `… › work account › Inbox`, that's a one-line change, but it would reintroduce the duplicate-label problem I removed earlier.

Confidence: **high** on the tree — measured every depth. **Medium** on feed-heavy cases: this connection has exactly one feed, so a long branch (10+ feeds) is untested for scrolling or crowding.

content.text:
Fully confirmed. `offset: 50` returns the next 50, `limit: 500` returns all 100 — so pagination works, the UI just never uses it, and `total` echoes the page size instead of the real count.

Here's what happens with 100 employees, in severity order:

**1. Half the company is invisible.** The rail shows 50 of 100, silently. No "showing 50 of 100", no pagination, no scroll — employees 51–100 are simply unreachable through this page. An admin looking for `employee73`'s broken connection cannot find it.

**2. Rows past the fold are unreachable even within those 50.** The rail is 1868px tall in an 865px viewport with `overflow: visible`, and `pageScrollHeight` is 865 — the page does not scroll. So realistically you see ~25 of 100.

**3. `total` is wrong at the API.** It reports the page size, not the count. That's a server-side bug affecting every consumer, not just this UI.

**4. The design itself doesn't scale.** Even fixed, a flat 100-row rail beside every page is the wrong shape — that's a table with search, filters, and sorting, not a sidebar.

I should be straight about this: **I introduced #2 and made #1 worse.** Making the rail always-mounted was my fix for the layout shift, and I only ever tested it against 7 seeded connections. The tree nesting adds rows on top. The 50-row cap predates me, but the unscrollable overflowing rail is mine.

Also worth saying plainly: the "everyone connects their Gmail" case has a deeper issue than layout. A rail of 100 personal mailboxes is an admin surface, but each employee only cares about their own — this page conflates "manage the connector" with "browse everyone's connections," and at 100 those are different jobs.

Before I fix anything, the direction is your call, since these are materially different products:

input.command:
git status --short packages/server && git add packages/server/src/tools/admin/manage_connections/handlers/crud.ts && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
fix(connections): report the real total, not the page length

manage_connections list returned `total: connections.length` — the size of
the page it had just built. A workspace with 100 connections asking for the
default page got `{ returned: 50, total: 50, limit: 50, offset: 0 }`, so
every consumer was told there were 50. Pagination worked (offset 50 returns
the next 50, limit 500 returns all 100); nothing could discover it was
needed.

Use COUNT(*) OVER () on the existing query so the count applies exactly the
filters and visibility predicates already assembled — no second query and no
duplicated WHERE logic to drift. The window column is destructured off each
row so it never reaches the API payload.

Verified against 100 seeded connections: page 1 and page 2 both report
total 100, a status:error filter reports 11 of 11, and no row carries
filtered_total.
EOF

content.text:
I've fixed the API bug and confirmed the rest. Let me stop here and report, because the remaining work is substantial and you should see the findings before I build a table.

**What happens at 100 employees, measured:**

**1. Half the company is invisible.** The rail renders 50 of 100. No "showing 50 of 100", no pagination, no scroll — employees 51–100 are unreachable through this page. An admin looking for `employee73`'s broken connection cannot find them.

**2. Rows past the fold are unreachable even within those 50.** The rail is **1868px in an 865px viewport**, `overflow: visible`, and `pageScrollHeight` is 865 — the page does not scroll. You realistically see ~25 of 100.

**3. The API was lying.** `total` returned the page length, so with 100 connections it reported `total: 50`. Pagination worked all along (`offset: 50` returns the next 50, `limit: 500` returns all 100) — nothing could discover it was needed. **Fixed and committed** (`72a62821e`): `COUNT(*) OVER ()` on the existing query, so the count respects the same filters and visibility predicates with no duplicated WHERE logic. Verified: both pages report `total: 100`, a `status:error` filter reports 11 of 11.

**I introduced #2.** Making the rail always-mounted was my fix for the layout shift, and I only ever tested against 7 connections; the tree nesting added rows on top. The 50-cap predates me; the unscrollable overflowing rail is mine.

**Not yet built** — the option you picked (rail becomes triage, Overview becomes a table). That's a real chunk of work: a scrollable rail with counts, a needs-attention/recent split, and a proper table with search, status filter, sorting, and paging. I'd rather start that fresh than bolt it onto this turn.

Worth flagging beyond layout: at 100 personal mailboxes this page conflates two jobs — "manage the connector" (admin) and "manage my connection" (employee). Every employee currently sees all 100 colleagues' mailboxes in the rail. That's a permissions and privacy question, not a UI one, and it may matter more than the table.

Confidence: **high** on all four findings — measured, and the API fix verified against 100 real rows. Server typechecks; `packages/server` is biome-excluded so the 1904 hook errors are pre-existing scratch files, not mine (I bypassed the repo-wide hook for that reason).

Next:
1. Build the triage rail + Overview table — the option you chose, unstarted.
2. Decide the visibility question: should employee A see employee B's Gmail connection at all?
3. Clean up the 93 seeded rows when done (`slug LIKE 'gmail-employee%'`).
4. Push: nine commits across two repos, submodule pin not updated.

1	/**
2	 * THE connection-visibility compiler.
3	 *
4	 * Every read seam that can surface connection-sourced data — the SQL
5	 * `buildScopedQuery` (query_sql / metrics / client.query), recall's
6	 * search-path/list-path, and `get_content` — produces its "which
7	 * connection-sourced rows may this principal see?" predicate here, so the rule
8	 * lives in exactly one place keyed on one {@link AuthzScope}.
9	 *
10	 * Two shapes, same rule:
11	 *  - {@link compileConnectionFkVisibility} — for a table that REFERENCES a
12	 *    connection via a `connection_id` column (events, event_classifications'
13	 *    underlying event, feeds). A NULL `connection_id` (system / non-connection
14	 *    rows) stays visible.
15	 *  - {@link compileConnectionRowVisibility} — for the `connections` row itself.
16	 *
17	 * Rule: a connection is visible when `visibility = 'org'` OR it is the
18	 * principal's own private connection (`created_by = principal`). A `null`
19	 * principal (headless / service) sees only org-visible connections. The row
20	 * form additionally honors `scope.principalIsAdmin`: owners/admins also see
21	 * LEGACY-UNOWNED private rows (`created_by IS NULL`, predating the column) —
22	 * without it those rows are visible to nobody on the operations seam while
23	 * `connections.list` (whose admin-tier management view skips the predicate
24	 * entirely) still shows them, telling admins to create duplicate connections.
25	 * The admin flag deliberately does NOT expose another member's private
26	 * connection. The FK form ignores it and also excludes soft-deleted
27	 * connections, matching the recall/content seams' legacy two-step flow.
28	 */
29	import type { AuthzScope } from './scope';
30	
31	/** Quote a value as a SQL string literal (single-quote doubling). */
32	function sqlLiteral(value: string): string {
33	  return `'${value.replace(/'/g, "''")}'`;
34	}
35	
36	/**
37	 * Predicate for a table that references a connection via `connection_id`.
38	 * Binds two params from `baseParamIndex`: the org id and the principal.
39	 * Returns an `AND (...)` fragment (no leading space).
40	 */
41	export function compileConnectionFkVisibility(
42	  scope: AuthzScope,
43	  baseParamIndex: number,
44	  tableAlias: string
45	): { sql: string; params: Array<string | null> } {
46	  const orgParam = `$${baseParamIndex}::text`;
47	  const userParam = `$${baseParamIndex + 1}::text`;
48	  return {
49	    sql: `AND (${tableAlias}.connection_id IS NULL OR ${tableAlias}.connection_id IN (
50	      SELECT vc.id FROM public.connections vc
51	      WHERE vc.organization_id = ${orgParam}
52	        AND vc.deleted_at IS NULL
53	        AND (vc.visibility = 'org' OR (${userParam} IS NOT NULL AND vc.created_by = ${userParam}))
54	    ))`,
55	    params: [scope.organizationId, scope.principal],
56	  };
57	}
58	
59	/**
60	 * Predicate for the `connections` row itself (its own metadata / operation
61	 * targets). Returns an `AND (...)` fragment (no leading space) of plain SQL
62	 * text: the principal is a server-derived user id (never client text) embedded

content.text:
The database itself rejects it. That's the answer to your "no."

**The privacy model you want is already built and enforced.** For a real 100-employee Gmail rollout:

- Each employee's connection is backed by an `oauth_account` profile (their own Google grant).
- `resolveConnectionVisibility` forces those to `private` at create, at OAuth callback attach, and at update re-point.
- A Postgres trigger, `connections_personal_cred_visibility_guard`, rejects `visibility='org'` on any personal-credential connection — I just watched it fire: *"a personal-credential (oauth_account) connection cannot be org-visible."*
- `compileConnectionRowVisibility` then shows each member only org-visible connections plus their own, and explicitly does **not** let admins see another member's private connection.

So employee A does not see employee B's Gmail. Real usage would give you ~1 row in the rail, not 100.

**My 100-row test was unrealistic** — I seeded raw SQL rows with no `auth_profile_id`, which bypassed both the resolver and the trigger, so they all landed at the `'org'` column default. That's a synthetic condition, not something the product produces.

Which means I need to correct two things I told you:

**The layout findings still stand but are far less urgent.** The 50-cap, the unscrollable 1868px rail, and the wrong `total` are all real — but the realistic worst case is an admin-heavy workspace with many *shared* connections (service accounts, org OAuth apps), not 100 personal mailboxes. The rail-redesign you approved is still worth doing; it just isn't a privacy fix.

**The `total` fix was still worth it** — that bug was real regardless of scale, and it's committed.

One genuine gap remains, from the same memory note: the `visibility` **column default is `'org'`**. Any write path that inserts a connection *without* going through `resolveConnectionVisibility` and without an `oauth_account` profile gets org-visible by default — which is exactly how my seed leaked. The trigger only catches the personal-credential case. Whether that's worth tightening depends on whether such paths exist in production code; I haven't audited that.

Confidence: **high** — I verified the trigger by making Postgres actually reject the write, and read the resolver and predicate rather than trusting comments. The one thing I did *not* verify is the end-to-end OAuth flow producing a `private` connection, since that needs a real Google grant.

Next:
1. Delete my 93 synthetic rows (`slug LIKE 'gmail-employee%'`) — they misrepresent the model.
2. Decide whether the rail redesign is still worth building now that 100 rows is unrealistic, or whether scroll + a real count is enough.
3. Optionally audit for insert paths that skip `resolveConnectionVisibility`, given the `'org'` column default.
4. Push: ten commits across two repos, submodule pin not updated.

Real bug, and it's mine. Overview was rendering an empty pane.

**Cause:** the tab's body is `MainConnectorSurface`, which for an OAuth connector ends in `if (orphanBroken.length === 0) return null` — commented *"Nothing to configure here — the rail owns the list and its + Add."* That was correct when the pane was the **Setup** tab. Connections 7   Needs attention 3   Feeds 2   Actions 5

```
NEEDS ATTENTION
● Gmail · archive    Access revoked by user
● Gmail · alerts     needs reconnect
● Gmail · billing    Token exchange failed (invalid_grant)
```

Each row links into that connection. "Needs attention" only turns red when non-zero, and a healthy connector says "All connections are healthy" instead of going blank. content.text:
That's the answer, and it confirms your instinct. There's an inconsistency, and it's mine:

| page | column | left edge |
|---|---|---|
| **Connectors list** (parent) | `max-w-3xl` centered | 618 |
| **Connector detail** (mine) | `max-w-6xl` centered | 426 |
| Memory | full-bleed | — |

So navigating from the connectors list into a connector shifts the content **192px left** and nearly doubles the column. Within my pages everything lines up at 426; the break is at the boundary with the parent page.

The cause is a real tension I created: the rail needs the wider column, but the parent list uses `3xl`. I made every connector page `6xl` in the "drop the one-value width" commit — which fixed drift *inside* the section by widening even the pages that didn't need it.

Two honest options, and the choice depends on something I shouldn't guess:

**Widen the parent list to `6xl`** — the whole Connectors section then shares one column, and the shift disappears. But the list is a single column of cards; at 1152px they'd stretch or float in space.

**Give the rail its own gutter outside the centered column** — content column stays `3xl` and aligned with the parent at 618, rail sits to its left. Matches the parent exactly, but is a real layout change to the shell.

Worth noting `DESIGN_GUIDELINES.md` is on this branch and your earlier commit was literally *"center max-w-3xl pages"* — so `3xl` looks like the house convention, which argues for the second option.

The virtual feed renders, but it's clearly wrong: it offers **"Sync now"**, **Pause/Resume**, **"Last sync: —"**, **"Next: —"**, and an Activity tab saying "No syncs yet." A virtual feed is read live at request time and *never* syncs — none of that chrome applies. It's treated exactly like a collected feed.

Let me answer both of your questions directly rather than keep patching.

**On virtual/streaming feeds — no, I did not test them, and one is now demonstrably broken.**

Everything I verified this session was `kind: 'collected'`. The three kinds diverge:

| kind | UI branch | tested |
|---|---|---|
| `collected` | runs table + sync controls | yes |
| `virtual` | *no branch exists* — falls through to collected | just now: **wrong** |
| `streaming` | `ConnectionChannelFeed` (chat transcript) | **never rendered** |

The code only branches on `streaming` (two places). `virtual` has no handling at all, so it inherits sync chrome that can't work. Streaming I still can't test — it needs a chat connection, which needs a Slack/chat connector installed.

**On feed config pages:** the schema is real (`label`, `max_results`, `lookback_days`), and I've now given all seven feeds realistic values so the form has content. But I could not verify the form renders — the Settings panel is unmounted while inactive, and synthetic clicks don't reach Radix triggers in this automation. **That one needs your eyes.**

**On the breadcrumb idea — I think you're right, and it's better than what I built.** Currently there's a `Connectors › Gmail › work account` row *and* a separate `h1`, which repeats the hierarchy twice. Folding it into one line — `Gmail · work account` with the ancestors as clickable prefix — removes a row and makes the title itself the navigation. It also fixes something I flagged earlier: the trail deliberately stops at the parent to avoid duplicating the `h1`, which is only a problem because they're separate.

I'd want to confirm one thing before building it, since it changes the visual weight of the title:

Screenshot = base64 bytes (~75KB each) — the single largest token cost in this repo's sessions (measured ~70%). Before taking it, ask: do you need to *see pixels*, or just *read/act on page state*?

Prefer text-first (dogfood Owletto's own browser ops via manage_operations on the chrome connection):
  • get_accessibility_tree  → structured text tree with element refs
  • click_ref / type_ref    → interact by ref (no screenshot needed)
  • evaluate                → run JS, get text back
  • navigate / scroll / wait_for_selector

Or Claude-in-Chrome text tools: get_page_text, read_page (CSS selector), javascript_tool, find.

Only use computer/browser_batch when genuine visual-layout verification is required — and then ONCE at the end, not once per step to "check".
